```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

A difference in life expectancy, between deprivation quintiles, between
two years or between two forecasts, is the sum of differences in death
rates at many ages and from many causes. A decomposition attributes it to
those ages and causes, and, for populations made of subgroups, separates
the effect of the subgroups' mortality from the effect of their
composition. In mortensor this is a post-processing step,
`mt_decompose()`, that works on observed data, on forecast draws, and on
both together. Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so every
contribution has an interval.

| Method | Decomposes | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `"arriaga"` (default for life expectancy) | life expectancy, by age (and cause) | Arriaga (1984), symmetric form as in Riffe et al. (2024) |
| `"horiuchi"` | any function of the rates | Horiuchi, Wilmoth and Pletcher (2008) |
| `"stepwise"` | any function of the rates | Andreev, Shkolnikov and Begun (2002) |
| `"kitagawa"` | crude death rate: rates and age structure | Kitagawa (1955) |
| `groups` with `composition = "radix"` | life expectancy of a population of subgroups fixed from the start (sex, education): subgroup rates and composition | Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024), "Arriaga meets Kitagawa" |
| `groups` with `composition = "pooled"` | life expectancy of the pooled rates (areas, regions): subgroup rates and age-specific composition | Horiuchi et al. (2008) |

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
x <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile"), age = "age_group",
             value = c(deaths = "all_causes", population = "population"))
x <- mt_as_exposure(x, type = "midyear")
x <- mt_group_levels(x, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
```

The data are the ONS deaths and populations of England by sex, 5-year age
group and IMD quintile, 2001-2019 (`ons_data`; Source: Office for National
Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0). Q1 is the most
deprived quintile.

## The deprivation gap by age

Each quintile compared with Q1 in 2019, with 200 Poisson draws of the
deaths for the intervals:

```{r}
gap <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, n_draws = 200)
gap
```

The totals list one comparison per row: the life expectancy of the
reference (`from_value`) and of the level (`to_value`), their difference
with its interval, and the sum of the age contributions, which equals the
difference (`max_residual` is the largest discrepancy over draws). Values
are means over the draws; quantiles are in the columns `difference_q*`
and in `summary()`. `summary(gap, by = "age")` gives the contributions;
the plot shows them for the gap between Q5 and Q1:

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_decomposition(gap, by = "age", comparisons = list(to = "Q5"))
```

```{r}
s <- summary(gap, by = "age")[to == "Q5"]
s[, band := cut(as.numeric(sub("[-+].*", "", age)), c(-1, 39, 64, 84, Inf),
                labels = c("0-39", "40-64", "65-84", "85+"))]
dcast(s[, .(contribution = round(sum(mean), 2)), by = .(sex, band)], sex ~ band, value.var = "contribution")
```

The gap of 6.5 years for women and 7.7 years for men comes mostly from
ages 40 to 84 (5.2 and 6.3 years): deaths at working ages and in early old
age are much more frequent in Q1. Ages below 40 add 0.6 years for women
and 0.9 years for men; infant mortality alone adds 0.2 years for women.
With Poisson draws of the observed deaths, the intervals of single ages
are narrow.

The methods agree closely. Symmetric Arriaga and symmetric stepwise
replacement are identical for life expectancy, because Arriaga's
decomposition is stepwise replacement from the oldest to the youngest age;
the line integral assigns interactions between ages slightly differently:

```{r}
meth <- rbindlist(lapply(c("arriaga", "horiuchi", "stepwise"), function(m) {
  d <- mt_decompose(x, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = 2019, method = m)
  summary(d, by = "age")[to == "Q5" & sex == "female", .(age, method = m, mean = round(mean, 3))]
}))
meth[, age := factor(age, unique(age))]
dcast(meth, age ~ method, value.var = "mean")[age %in% c("0", "40-44", "60-64", "75-79", "90+")]
```

## Causes behind the gap

Causes of death are a stratum variable whose rates add up to all causes.
`cause` names it. The total level (`"all"`) is left out because
`mt_group_levels(total = "all")` records it in the data; without such a
record (or a `hierarchy`), `mt_decompose()` stops rather than count all
causes as one more cause. At ages 50 and over (as in "Causes of death by
deprivation"):

```{r}
causes <- names(ons_data)[-(1:7)]
xc <- mt_data(deaths = ons_data, population = ons_data, by = c("sex", "imd_decile", "cause"),
              age = "age_group", value = list(deaths = c(all = "all_causes", causes), population = "population"))
xc <- mt_as_exposure(xc, type = "midyear")
xc <- mt_subset(xc, ages = c(50, Inf), periods = c(2019, 2019))
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "imd_decile", function(d) paste0("Q", ceiling(as.numeric(d) / 2)), name = "quintile")
xc <- mt_group_levels(xc, "cause", ons_cause_groups, other = "rest", total = "all", additive = "rates")
gc <- mt_decompose(xc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", cause = "cause")
sc <- summary(gc, by = "cause")[to == "Q5"]
dcast(sc, cause ~ sex, value.var = "mean")[order(-female), lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v, 2) else v)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 5.5}
mt_plot_decomposition(gc, by = "age", fill = "cause", comparisons = list(to = "Q5"))
```

Each age contribution is split over the causes in proportion to their
rate differences (Riffe et al. 2024, eqs. 12-13). Of the gap in life
expectancy at 50, respiratory diseases, lung cancer and ischaemic heart
disease contribute most among the named causes, for both sexes, and the
remaining causes together (`rest`) contribute a large share. Causes with
higher rates in Q5 than in Q1 would have negative contributions.

## Change over time and the composition of England

The life expectancy of a population of subgroups changes because the
mortality of every subgroup changes and because the population shifts
between subgroups. `groups` names the subgroups, and `composition` decides
which life expectancy of the whole population is decomposed. The choice
matters, so it has no default.

**Subgroups fixed from the start of life: `composition = "radix"`.**
Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós (2024) treat the life expectancy of a
population as the mean of the subgroups' life expectancies, weighted by
their shares at the starting age, as if subgroup life tables were blended
at the radix. A Kitagawa decomposition of that mean separates the
composition from the change within each subgroup, which is then split by
age. The authors state the condition: membership must be fixed from the
starting age on, and later shares must change through mortality only, as
for sex, education from age 30 or country of birth. Sex is such a
subgroup: the life expectancy at birth of both sexes in each quintile,
with the sex ratio at birth as the composition:

```{r}
both <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "sex", composition = "radix")
both
summary(both, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(quintile, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
```

The printout states what the values are: means of women's and men's life
expectancy weighted by the sex ratio at birth, not the life expectancy of
the pooled rates. In every quintile men contributed more to the rise than
women (in Q1 1.9 against 1.1 years); the sex ratio at birth hardly changed,
so its composition effect is a few hundredths of a year.

**Areas and other changing groups: `composition = "pooled"`.** Deprivation
quintiles are areas: people move between them, and areas change quintile
with each IMD version. The condition of the radix version does not hold.
The pooled version decomposes the life expectancy of the pooled rates of
England (the quintiles weighted by their population at each age, as in
published life tables; "current rates" in Vaupel's terms, which Riffe et
al. use, against "current conditions" for the radix version). The rates of
every quintile and age and the shares at every age are the parameters of a
line-integral decomposition:

```{r}
eng <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile", composition = "pooled")
eng
summary(eng, by = c("component", "group"))[, .(sex, component, group, mean = round(mean, 3))]
```

Life expectancy at birth of England rose by 3.0 years for women and 4.0
years for men. Every quintile contributed about half a year or more; for
men, Q1 contributed most. The composition effect is positive and small
(0.10 and 0.03 years). Applied to the quintiles, the radix version would
give a negative composition effect, because the shares at birth and at
older ages moved in opposite directions:

```{r}
eng_radix <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), groups = "quintile", composition = "radix")
rbind(summary(eng, by = "component")[, .(composition = "pooled", sex, component, mean = round(mean, 3))],
      summary(eng_radix, by = "component")[, .(composition = "radix", sex, component, mean = round(mean, 3))])
E <- mt_array(x, "exposure")
women <- x$strata$label[x$strata$sex == "female"]
round(rbind(birth_2001 = E["0", "2001", women], birth_2019 = E["0", "2019", women],
            age75_2001 = E["75-79", "2001", women], age75_2019 = E["75-79", "2019", women]) /
        rep(c(sum(E["0", "2001", women]), sum(E["0", "2019", women]), sum(E["75-79", "2001", women]),
              sum(E["75-79", "2019", women])), 5), 3)
```

At birth the share of Q5 fell (from 18% to 16% for girls), while at ages
75-79, where many deaths occur, it rose from 19% to 24% and the share of
Q1 fell from 19% to 14%. The radix version treats the shares at birth as
the composition of the whole population, which is wrong for areas. The
composition effect is a single number (radix) or one per age (pooled):
the separate composition terms of the subgroups are not identified.

## Forecasts

Li-Lee forecasts to 2035, decomposed draw by draw. With draws, `periods`
can combine an observed year (held in the draws) with forecast years:

```{r}
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
change <- mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2019, 2035))
summary(change, by = NULL)[, .(sex, quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, jump_off)]
```

A change from an observed to a forecast year contains the step from the
observed rates of 2019 to the model's fitted rates of 2019 (the jump-off,
see `mt_jump_off()`), and with it the noise of the observed year. Column
`jump_off` gives its share: of the forecast gain of 3.5 years for women in
Q1, 0.4 years come from this step. `observed = "fitted"` decomposes the
model's change alone:

```{r}
change_fit <- mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2019, 2035), observed = "fitted")
summary(change_fit, by = NULL)[, .(sex, quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, difference_q0.025,
                                   difference_q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_decomposition(change_fit, by = "age", comparisons = list(quintile = "Q1"))
```

The model's gain for women in Q1 (3.1 years) comes mostly from ages 50 to
84. The bars give the mean contribution and the lines the 95% interval of
each age over the draws. The intervals are wide and include zero at most
ages: the common trend of Li-Lee is uncertain 16 years ahead, and it moves
all ages together, so the uncertainty of the ages adds up in the total.
`observed = "poisson"` would add the sampling uncertainty of the observed
year.

The gap between Q5 and Q1 in 2019 and in 2035, and its change. For the
change, `summary(change = )` subtracts the two decompositions draw by
draw:

```{r}
g <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035))
summary(g, by = NULL)[to == "Q5", .(sex, period, difference, difference_q0.025, difference_q0.975, jump_off)]
g_fit <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "quintile", ref = "Q1", periods = c(2019, 2035), observed = "fitted")
summary(g_fit, by = NULL, change = c(2019, 2035))[to == "Q5", .(sex, period, from_value, to_value, difference,
                                                                difference_q0.025, difference_q0.975)]
ch <- summary(g_fit, by = "age", change = c(2019, 2035))[to == "Q5" & sex == "female"]
ch[, band := cut(as.numeric(sub("[-+].*", "", age)), c(-1, 39, 59, 84, Inf),
                 labels = c("0-39", "40-59", "60-84", "85+"))]
ch[, .(change = round(sum(mean), 2)), by = band]
```

Li-Lee forecasts a female gap of 4.6 years in 2035, against 6.5 observed in
2019. Of this narrowing of 1.9 years, 0.8 years is the jump-off: the Li-Lee
fit of 2019 already puts the gap at 5.7 years. The model's own narrowing,
from the fitted 2019 gap, is 1.1 years (95% interval 0.03 to 2.0), 0.8 of
it at ages 60 to 84, where the deviations of Q1 from the common trend
return towards their average (see "Forecasting mortality by deprivation
quintile"). `anchored()` moves the start towards the observed level but
fades out within ten years, so it does not change the gap in 2035.

Two forecasts of the same year are compared by giving the second as `y`.
Their draws are independent, so they are shuffled before they are paired
(`pairing = "independent"`). Lee-Carter per quintile against Li-Lee, for
2035:

```{r}
fl <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), to = 2035, n_draws = 500, seed = 1)
mm <- mt_decompose(fc, fl, periods = 2035)
summary(mm, by = NULL)[sex == "female", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference, difference_q0.025,
                                          difference_q0.975)]
```

```{r, eval = has_gg}
mt_plot_decomposition(mm, by = "age", comparisons = list(quintile = "Q1"))
```

For women in Q1, Lee-Carter forecasts 1.9 years less than Li-Lee, 1.7
years of it at ages 60 and over: Lee-Carter extrapolates the slower
improvement of Q1 at these ages in 2001-2019, while Li-Lee lets Q1 return
towards the common trend of all quintiles. The interval of the difference
is wide because both forecasts are uncertain; it says how different two
independent forecasts can be, not how different the models are.

## Other quantities

`quantity` selects the summary. The probability of dying between 30 and
75 and the age-standardised rate are decomposed by age with the line
integral; any function of the rates can be given as well:

```{r}
pd <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "prob_dying", at = 30, to = 75)
summary(pd, by = NULL)[sex == "male", .(quintile, from_value, to_value, difference)]
```

The crude death rate changes with the rates and with the age structure of
the population. Kitagawa's decomposition separates the two:

```{r}
cr <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2001, 2019), quantity = "crude_rate")
dcast(summary(cr, by = "component"), sex + quintile ~ component, value.var = "mean")[
  , lapply(.SD, function(v) if (is.numeric(v)) round(v) else v)]
```

Per 100,000, falling rates lowered the crude death rate of every quintile
by 140 to 360 deaths. Ageing raised it, most in the least deprived
quintiles, whose populations are oldest; only for women in Q1 and Q2 did
the age structure lower it. For men in Q5 the crude rate rose although the
rates fell.

## Choosing a method

* Life expectancy by age and cause: `"arriaga"` (exact and fast). Other
  quantities: `"horiuchi"` or `"stepwise"`; the line integral distributes
  interactions evenly, stepwise replacement depends on the order of the
  ages.
* Populations of subgroups: `composition = "radix"` (Riffe et al.) for
  subgroups fixed from the starting age (sex, education from 30 or 35,
  country of birth); `"pooled"` for areas, regions and other groups
  between which people move, and whenever the target is the life
  expectancy of the whole population as published.
* Forecasts from an observed year: report the jump-off (`jump_off`) or
  decompose from the fitted rates (`observed = "fitted"`); compare two
  models with independent draws (the default).
* Forecasts: contributions and their sums come with intervals, because
  every draw is decomposed. Sums over ages or causes are formed draw by
  draw (`summary(by = )`), so their intervals are not sums of intervals.
* Cause-specific contributions are only as good as the coding of causes;
  trends in coding (dementia, ill-defined causes) move between causes, not
  in the total.

## References

Andreev EM, Shkolnikov VM, Begun AZ (2002). Algorithm for decomposition of
differences between aggregate demographic measures and its application to
life expectancies, healthy life expectancies, parity-progression ratios and
total fertility rates. *Demographic Research* 7: 499-522.

Arriaga EE (1984). Measuring and explaining the change in life
expectancies. *Demography* 21(1): 83-96.

Horiuchi S, Wilmoth JR, Pletcher SD (2008). A decomposition method based on
a model of continuous change. *Demography* 45(4): 785-801.

Kitagawa EM (1955). Components of a difference between two rates. *Journal
of the American Statistical Association* 50(272): 1168-1194.

Riffe T, Tursun-zade R, Trias Llimós S (2024). Arriaga meets Kitagawa. Life
expectancy decomposition with population subgroups. MPIDR Working Paper
WP-2024-029. doi:10.4054/MPIDR-WP-2024-029. Published in *Geographical
Analysis* (2026), doi:10.1111/gean.70033. Equation numbers in this
package refer to the working paper.

Vaupel JW (2002). Life expectancy at current rates vs. current conditions:
a reflexion stimulated by Bongaarts and Feeney's "How long do we live?".
*Demographic Research* 7: 365-378.
